task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper reported feature for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of March 18, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Areteia Pharma, a antibiotics-focused company with 34 employees, has three antibiotic candidates in clinical development and is running on 14 months of cash as of March 2025.
The company has not launched a commercial product; it generates no revenue from drug sales and depends entirely on grant funding and investor backing.

Areteia CEO Dr. Carlos Fuentes said: "We have drugs that work against bacteria that nothing else kills. We cannot raise the Series C to bring them to market. That is not a scientific failure. It is an economic failure."

Infectious disease specialist Dr. Josephine Amin said the Areteia situation is representative: the WHO's 2024 pipeline assessment found only 12 antibiotics in Phase 3 trials globally, of which four address priority resistant pathogens.
Dr. Amin said: "The pipeline is not empty. It is not funded. There is a difference. The science works. The business model doesn't."

The core economic problem: a new antibiotic approved today would be used sparingly to delay resistance — good medical practice, but it means sales volumes stay low and the company cannot recover its development cost.
Two antibiotic startups that reached Phase 3 trials in the United States between 2018 and 2023 declared bankruptcy after approval; their drugs remained available but production nearly ceased.

Fuentes said Areteia's most advanced candidate targets Acinetobacter baumannii, a gram-negative bacterium responsible for severe hospital infections and classified by the WHO as a critical priority pathogen.
A Phase 2 trial showed the drug cleared the pathogen in 14 of 18 patients whose infections had not responded to any other antibiotic; the trial was too small to be statistically definitive.

Dr. Amin said the Phase 2 data is scientifically encouraging but insufficient for FDA approval; reaching Phase 3 requires $60 to $90 million, which Fuentes said Areteia cannot raise under current market conditions.
The U.S. PASTEUR Act, which would create a subscription payment model to compensate antibiotic developers based on availability rather than volume, has passed committee but not been enacted.
Under PASTEUR, the government would pay companies up to $3 billion over 10 years for maintaining an approved antibiotic available for use, regardless of how many prescriptions are written.
Fuentes said Areteia cannot wait for PASTEUR: "It's been in Congress for four years. We have 14 months. Legislation that hasn't passed doesn't pay salaries."

Dr. Amin said she has seen three promising antibiotic programs discontinued in the past decade for economic reasons, not scientific ones: "It is a preventable loss. We are choosing not to prevent it."
The National Institutes of Health provided $14 million in preclinical funding to Areteia's lead candidate; private investors have contributed $38 million across two funding rounds.
Fuentes said the company is in conversations with two large pharmaceutical companies about licensing the Acinetobacter program; neither has made a formal offer.

Large pharmaceutical companies exited antibiotic research in the 2010s because the returns did not justify the investment; several have said they would re-enter if pull incentive programs were enacted.

Dr. Amin said the gap between scientific readiness and commercial viability in antibiotics is not new: it has been documented since the early 2000s and has not been resolved by any policy response so far.

Fuentes said he will not describe the situation as hopeless: "The drugs work. The need is real. We are one policy decision or one partnership away from a different outcome. That's both encouraging and maddening."

Dr. Amin said the final irony is that if Areteia fails, its compound could disappear even if the clinical data would have supported approval: "It takes more than science to save a drug. It takes money and timing and luck, which is a terrible way to manage a public health emergency."
